reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a consumer-finance tutorial on finding discounted iTunes gift cards and applying the balance toward a Netflix subscription. The visible Apple and Netflix screens match the described redemption and subscription steps, and the request to subscribe and comment is ordinary audience engagement rather than a condition for receiving money. The material does not describe solicitation of investments, private credentials, or payment to the speaker.

citations.quote: How to save 15% on Netflix using Itunes Gift Card
Step by step guide from finding discounted iTunes gift card to using it for Netflix.
these deals to buy a discount on iTunes gift card happens all the time
I bought this gift card, $100 gift card for $85 from Costco
The first step is to buy the discounted gift card.

opening.argument: The video links a promised saving directly to a purchase-and-redemption workflow. It promises to save viewers “15% or more” on Netflix, then instructs them to buy a discounted iTunes gift card, load it into an Apple account, and subscribe through iTunes. That is not merely discussion of discounts: the benefit is presented as contingent on acquiring the gift card and completing the subscription flow. The viewer is also directed to create an account and set an alert on Slickdeals so future offers can be pursued. The result is a solicitation to obtain and use a stored-value asset in order to receive the advertised saving, while the video does not establish that the discount will be consistently available or that every viewer will qualify.

citations.quote: How to save 15% on Netflix using Itunes Gift Card
I'm gonna show you how to save 15% or more on your Netflix subscription using iTunes gift card
The first step is to buy the discounted gift card.
Go to slickdeals.com, make an account, and set a deal alert for iTunes gift card.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a tutorial does not remove the solicitation. The title and narration pair a concrete saving claim with instructions to buy gift cards, register on an external deal site, and route a Netflix subscription through Apple. The screens show that a subscription flow exists, but they do not establish that the advertised 15% saving is available to the viewer, ongoing, or risk-free. Ordinary audience engagement is beside the point: the actionable purchase pathway is the central content.

citations.quote: Go to slickdeals.com, make an account, and set a deal alert for iTunes gift card.
The first step is to buy the discounted gift card.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted steps show an ordinary discount mechanism, not a low-barrier reward scam. The viewer buys a gift card from a retailer and uses its balance for a subscription; no free money, payout, or claim fee is promised. The video also limits the method by stating that an Apple device is required. The cited purchase instructions therefore describe consumer spending to obtain a discount, not evidence that the promised benefit is deceptive or that the gift card is acquired without equivalent payment.

citations.quote: you do need to have an Apple device like an iPhone or an iPad where you can subscribe Netflix through iTunes
I bought this gift card, $100 gift card for $85 from Costco
Step by step guide from finding discounted iTunes gift card to using it for Netflix.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: a promised 15% or greater return on an ordinary subscription expense, repeated references to discounted gift cards, an external website used to locate offers, and a personal success example presented as reassurance. The speaker says he saw nine deals in three months and reports buying a $100 card for $85, which makes the saving sound readily repeatable. Yet the viewer is told to monitor Slickdeals, buy the card when an offer appears, load it into an Apple account, and use it for Netflix. Gift cards are stored-value instruments, so the viewer must commit money before discovering whether the relevant offer, device, account, or subscription path works. The evidence supports concern about an attractive but conditional acquisition pitch, not a guaranteed universal saving.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats retailer names and a receipt image as if they validate the offer for all viewers. They do not. A past purchase and a displayed charge establish only that one example occurred; they do not establish a continuing 15% saving, universal eligibility, or that the viewer can safely reproduce it. The external alert and gift-card steps remain a participation funnel, and the Apple subscription screen confirms payment authorization rather than the claimed discount.

citations.quote: I bought this gift card, $100 gift card for $85 from Costco last February 2018.
if you get it at a discount rate, you'll get a discounted Netflix account as well

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary limitations of a retail promotion, not scam indicators. The speaker identifies named retailers, gives a dated personal example, and explains that the discount depends on obtaining a discounted card. The material does not promise guaranteed availability or claim that viewers receive cash; it describes using a lower-cost payment method. A receipt and subscription screen are relevant corroboration of the described process, even if they cannot guarantee future promotions.

opening.argument: Although presented as education, the video functions as a promotion directing viewers toward a particular acquisition behavior. It repeatedly tells viewers where to search, how to create an account and alert, how to redeem the card, and how to authorize Netflix through iTunes. The speaker also asks viewers to subscribe and comment after demonstrating the process. The framing as frugal advice makes the commercial-style message more persuasive: buy a stored-value Apple card, use it for a subscription, and expect a lower price. The supplied description itself calls this a step-by-step guide, while the title foregrounds the promised saving. That combination steers participation rather than neutrally explaining an existing transaction.

So thank you guys for watching. If you want to hear more videos to save money, please hit the subscribe button

rebuttal.rebuttal: The educational label describes format, not effect. The video does more than explain that discounts exist: it names a search service, tells viewers to create an account and alerts, demonstrates gift-card redemption, and directs them toward an Apple-billed Netflix subscription. The visible Apple and Netflix interfaces show implementation, but they do not change the fact that the content is organized to move viewers toward purchasing and authorizing a payment method.

citations.quote: Go to slickdeals.com, make an account, and set a deal alert Slick Deals.
now the key here is subscribe with itunes

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Instructional detail is exactly what a legitimate consumer tutorial requires. The guide explains a lawful retail discount, shows redemption through the App Store, and identifies that the method can apply to Netflix and other apps. The request to subscribe to the creator's channel does not condition the financial benefit, and the evidence contains no demand to send money to the speaker or disclose sensitive information. Promotion of a money-saving technique is not itself a fraudulent acquisition scheme.
